strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: enabling training-free video reasoning segmentation by probing intrinsic MLLM localization ability, avoiding costly LoRA/SAM co-training pipelines used by prior work.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL/2.5VL) and five datasets (three referring VOS, two reasoning VOS), which supports the generality claims better than a single-model, single-dataset study.

Thorough and honest reproducibility analysis of baselines: the paper carefully documents why Loc-Head's heuristics (bottom-row exclusion, RefCOCO-based head discovery) and TAM's token-dependence fail to generalize to the video/reasoning setting, lending credibility to the comparisons.

Comprehensive ablations (contrastive fusion, video-frame fusion, multi-scale complementing, rollout normalization, SAM prompting thresholds, consistency score design, MLLM scaling) that isolate the contribution of each proposed component and show consistent, non-trivial gains.

Achieves performance competitive with (and sometimes exceeding) training-based methods (VISA, VideoLISA, and close to GLUS/Veason-R1) despite requiring no fine-tuning, which is a meaningful practical result.
Includes candid failure-case analysis (thin/elongated objects, small transient objects, attention-consistency penalty edge cases), improving transparency about the method's limitations.
weaknesses: The pipeline is fairly complex and introduces many hand-tuned hyperparameters (τpq, τtrk, NMS IoU=0.7, rollout starting layer, Gaussian smoothing, Otsu vs. mean thresholding for s^ac) that are themselves heuristic choices, somewhat undercutting the paper's central critique of Loc-Head for relying on heuristics.

No analysis of computational cost/inference latency is provided; the method requires multiple additional forward passes per video (object-focused prompt, background-focused prompt, video-level and frame-level rollout, SAM2 point-prompt propagation), which could make it substantially slower than single-pass training-based approaches despite being 'training-free.'

Absolute performance of attention-only masks (Table 1) remains quite low (J&F often in the teens-to-twenties), and contour accuracy (F) is notably weaker than region similarity (J), indicating the core attention-based localization signal is still coarse and only becomes competitive after heavy SAM2 post-processing.

The optimal starting layer for rollout and threshold values vary by model/dataset (Table 5b, Table 6), suggesting some residual model-specific tuning is still needed despite claims of a unified, model-agnostic framework.
Limited evaluation of multi-object scenarios beyond qualitative examples; no dedicated quantitative benchmark or metric specifically targeting multi-object disambiguation performance.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: individual components (attention rollout, contrastive prompting, multi-scale fusion, SAM-guided prompting) are combinations/adaptations of existing ideas rather than fundamentally new mechanisms, and the primary contribution is largely engineering/empirical rather than conceptual.

Only 16 uniformly sampled frames are used in main experiments; there is no analysis of sensitivity to frame sampling density or performance on longer videos, which limits confidence in scalability claims.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: avoiding costly LoRA fine-tuning and joint SAM training for video reasoning segmentation by exploiting MLLMs' intrinsic attention signals.

Broad empirical evaluation across three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5VL) and five datasets (referring and reasoning VOS), which is more comprehensive than most training-free grounding papers.

Careful, honest failure analysis of competing training-free methods (TAM's token-dependence, Loc-Head's heuristic fragility across models) that is backed by reproduced experiments, adding credibility to the comparisons.

Extensive ablation studies (Tables 4-8) isolating the contribution of each component (contrastive fusion, complementary fusion, rollout normalization, SAM prompting thresholds, consistency scoring), showing the pipeline is reasonably well understood.
Clear, well-illustrated figures (attention maps, pipeline diagrams) that aid understanding of the proposed mechanisms.
Transparent reporting of failure cases (thin/elongated objects, brief appearances of small objects) in the appendix rather than only showcasing favorable qualitative results.
weaknesses: The claim of achieving performance 'comparable to training-based methods' is overstated: on several benchmarks (e.g., ReVOS Overall 50.3 vs. VRS-HQ 59.1 and Veason-R1 61.3; MeViS 43.5 vs. GLUS 51.3 and VRS-HQ 50.6) the gap is still 8-11 J&F points, which is substantial rather than 'comparable.'

The method's 'training-free' simplicity is undermined by heavy reliance on multiple hand-crafted prompt templates (object-focused, background-focused, category-choice prompts) and several tuned hyperparameters (τpq, τtrk, Gaussian smoothing, Otsu thresholding, rollout starting layer), which is conceptually similar to the heuristic dependence the paper criticizes in Loc-Head, just moved into prompt engineering rather than head selection.

No analysis of computational cost/runtime: the pipeline requires multiple separate MLLM forward passes per video (object prompt, background prompt, video-level and frame-level attention per frame) plus iterative SAM2 point-prompt propagation and NMS, which likely incurs substantial inference overhead versus training-based single-pass methods, yet this trade-off is not quantified.

Accuracy of the pipeline hinges on correct object-category prediction from the LLM (used to build the background-focused prompt); no quantitative analysis is given on how often this category prediction fails and how errors propagate to final segmentation quality.

Technical novelty is incremental: the core building blocks (attention rollout, contrastive prompting for background suppression, point-prompt-based SAM conditioning) are each adaptations of existing ideas (Abnar & Zuidema rollout, VL-SAM/TAM-style attention-to-mask conversion), and the main contribution is their combination and tuning rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Reported reproduction issues for baselines (Loc-Head drastically changes performance depending on sampling source for head discovery, tiling settings, heuristic column/row exclusion) raise questions about whether the baseline comparisons are entirely fair or whether the authors' reproduction choices inadvertently favor their own method.
No code is released at submission time (only promised), and given the many implementation-specific choices described, reproducibility is a concern without access to exact prompts/thresholds/code.

Absolute performance on attention-mask-only setting (Table 1) remains quite low (teens in J&F) even though relatively better than baselines, indicating the core attention-based localization signal is still weak and most of the final gains come from the SAM2 prompting/scoring engineering rather than the attention fusion itself.

Limited discussion of variance/statistical significance across runs or random seeds, and no analysis of sensitivity to the quality/architecture differences across the three MLLM backbones beyond a single scalability table.

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: training-free video reasoning segmentation, avoiding costly MLLM+SAM joint finetuning that existing methods require.

The proposed Decomposed Attention Fusion (DecAF) is conceptually simple yet effective, combining contrastive object-background fusion and complementary video-frame fusion to denoise attention rollout maps, with intuitive motivations grounded in observed phenomena (visual attention sink, softmax normalization effects across video vs. frame tokens).

Thorough empirical evaluation across three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL/2.5VL) and five datasets (three referring VOS, two reasoning VOS), showing consistent improvements over training-free baselines (TAM, Loc-Head) and performance competitive with several training-based methods.

Extensive and well-organized ablation studies covering each fusion component, rollout normalization scheme, layer selection, SAM prompting thresholds, and the attention consistency scoring mechanism, which support the design choices convincingly.

Careful and transparent analysis of why prior training-free baselines (TAM, Loc-Head) fail to generalize, including reproduction details, hyperparameter sensitivity, and documented limitations (e.g., Loc-Head's heuristic head-exclusion not transferring across MLLMs), strengthening the credibility of comparisons.

Good discussion of failure cases (thin/elongated objects, small/brief-appearing objects, inconsistent attention coverage) that provides useful insight into current method limitations and avenues for future work.

The attention-guided SAM2 prompting pipeline with tracklet scoring (object score + attention consistency score) is a reasonable practical contribution that bridges coarse attention maps to dense, fine-grained masks without any training.
weaknesses: Despite claims of being 'model- and task-agnostic,' the method still relies on several carefully engineered heuristics (fixed prompt templates, threshold values τpq/τtrk, choice of middle rollout layer, Gaussian smoothing, Otsu vs mean thresholding) that required dataset/model-specific tuning in ablations, somewhat undercutting the 'training-free generalizes cleanly' narrative.

Performance still lags behind state-of-the-art training-based methods on several benchmarks (e.g., VRS-HQ, Veason-R1, GLUS on MeViS and ReVOS), and the paper's claim of being 'comparable' is sometimes optimistic given consistent gaps of several points.

The method requires multiple additional forward passes through the MLLM (object-focused prompt, background-focused prompt, video-level pass, frame-level pass per frame) which likely incurs non-trivial inference-time computational overhead; this cost is not quantified or compared against baselines in terms of runtime/latency.

No analysis of sensitivity to the accuracy of the predicted object category (used for contrastive background prompting); errors in this single-word category prediction could propagate and degrade the whole pipeline, but this failure mode is not explicitly studied quantitatively.

The paper lacks comparison/discussion of computational cost and scalability with longer videos (e.g., runtime, memory, or frame-count scaling for attention rollout and SAM2 propagation), which is relevant for practical deployment.

Some presentation issues: figures are described in detail but actual quantitative qualitative comparison metrics for the failure-case videos are not given, and the main tables are dense, making cross-dataset trends slightly difficult to parse at a glance.

strengths: Extensive empirical validation across three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5VL) and five datasets (referring and reasoning VOS), with consistent improvements over training-free baselines (Loc-Head, TAM) and performance competitive with or exceeding several training-based methods, which is a notable result for a purely training-free pipeline.

Clear, well-motivated decomposition of the problem into two intuitive fusion mechanisms (contrastive object-background and complementary video-frame), each independently ablated and shown to contribute meaningfully to performance (Tables 4-5).

Thorough ablation studies covering rollout normalization, layer selection, SAM prompting thresholds, and the attention consistency scoring mechanism, indicating careful engineering and analysis of design choices.

Very extensive appendix with failure case analysis, prompt robustness studies (three prompt variants for each of the three prompt types), part-level segmentation exploration, non-explicit/implicit object expression cases, and detailed critique/reproduction analysis of baseline methods (Loc-Head, TAM), which strengthens confidence in the reported comparisons and reproducibility.

The method is conceptually simple (rollout + subtraction + averaging + thresholding) and requires no additional training, making it broadly applicable and easy to adopt across different MLLM backbones.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (attention rollout, contrastive prompting for saliency, multi-scale fusion, point-prompting SAM) are each individually well-established; the contribution is primarily a careful combination and engineering of these existing ideas for a new task setting rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The pipeline is fairly complex and relies on many hand-tuned components and thresholds (τpq, τtrk, Gaussian smoothing, Otsu vs. mean thresholding, NMS overlap threshold, per-frame vs global normalization), raising concerns about how well these choices transfer to unseen domains beyond the tested benchmarks, despite the robustness ablations provided.

The method requires multiple separate MLLM forward passes per video (object-focused, background-focused, category-choice, video-level, and frame-level per-frame queries), which likely introduces significant computational/inference overhead compared to a single-pass captioning/QA baseline; this cost is not clearly quantified or compared against baselines.

Absolute performance on the more complex reasoning benchmarks (ReVOS, ReasonVOS) remains substantially lower than top training-based methods (e.g., Veason-R1, VRS-HQ) in several settings, and the paper's own results show clear degradation on challenging sub-cases like multiple similar objects, small/thin objects, and part-level segmentation (acknowledged in appendix), suggesting the practical robustness gains are still limited for hard cases.

The correctness of the whole contrastive fusion pipeline hinges on accurately inferring a single object category name from the expression, which may be fragile for expressions with multiple targets, ambiguous references, or when the query does not map cleanly to a single noun (e.g., non-explicit expressions rely on similar category inference)—the paper shows successful qualitative cases but does not quantify how often/why this step fails at scale.

Some baseline reproduction gaps are large and rely on the authors' own reimplementation and heuristics (e.g., Loc-Head's SAM prompting score dropping from 74.2 to 34.4 upon reproduction), which, while explained, makes exact quantitative comparisons somewhat dependent on the authors' interpretation of baseline settings.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2/2.5VL) and five VOS benchmarks (referring and reasoning), with thorough ablations (rollout normalization, layer choice, contrastive/complementary fusion components, SAM prompting thresholds, tracklet scoring) that clarify which design choices matter.

The training-free setting is a practically appealing angle, and the paper carefully diagnoses failure modes of prior training-free baselines (TAM's token-decoding instability, Loc-Head's head-selection heuristics not transferring across models/datasets), providing useful negative results for the community.

On the more reasoning-heavy benchmark (ReasonVOS) the method surpasses several training-based baselines, including one that additionally performs RL fine-tuning on the same backbone, suggesting the fused attention maps do capture some of the MLLM's reasoning signal.

Very extensive appendix (prompt-robustness study, native-grounding baseline comparisons, part-level and non-explicit-object qualitative analyses, failure case gallery) demonstrating an unusually thorough attempt at self-scrutiny.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a combination of largely known ingredients (attention rollout, contrastive prompting/subtraction to suppress background, multi-scale/video-frame averaging, SAM point-prompting with NMS and consistency filtering); the novelty is incremental engineering on top of existing rollout- and Loc-Head-style pipelines rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The pipeline is heavily hand-tuned with numerous heuristic components and thresholds (τpq, τtrk, Otsu vs. mean thresholding, NMS IoU cutoff, Gaussian smoothing, multi-scale tiling rules that differ per MLLM family) — this undercuts the 'simple and effective' framing and raises reproducibility/generalization concerns for MLLMs not covered in the paper.

Computational cost is never quantified. The method requires multiple separate MLLM forward passes per video (object-focused, background-focused, category-choice, per-frame image-level, and video-level attention extraction) plus SAM2 propagation with many candidate point queries — this is likely far more expensive at inference than a single trained model, yet the efficiency argument against training-based methods is only framed qualitatively.

Results are inconsistent: on Ref-DAVIS with InternVL3-8B, Loc-Head still slightly outperforms DecAF, and on ReVOS the method trails recent training-based SOTA (e.g., Veason-R1, VRS-HQ) by a sizable margin, weakening the claim of being 'comparable to training-based methods' across the board.

Without SAM, absolute segmentation quality remains very low (J&F in the 13–25 range), and contour accuracy (F) remains persistently weaker than region similarity (J) even after SAM refinement — the coarse attention signal is acknowledged but the paper does not offer a solution beyond point-prompting SAM, limiting the practical utility of the 'direct attention mask' contribution that is emphasized in the abstract.

The attention consistency score and mask tracklet scoring, while ablated, are somewhat ad hoc (mean-thresholding + penalty term is chosen because it 'happens to work better'), and failure cases (Fig. 9) show it can incorrectly filter out valid small/thin/large-object tracklets, indicating limited robustness of a key component.

Reasoning-VOS test sets used for zero-shot evaluation (e.g., ReasonVOS) are relatively small, and no variance/multiple-seed analysis is reported despite the method's dependence on many stochastic-ish thresholding and prompt-based steps.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated training-free approach that decomposes attention rollout into contrastive object-background and complementary video-frame fusion, directly addressing the visual attention sink problem identified in prior work.

Extensive experimental validation across three MLLM families (LLaVA-OV, InternVL3, Qwen2VL/2.5VL) and five datasets (three referring VOS, two reasoning VOS), demonstrating consistent improvements over training-free baselines (Loc-Head, TAM).

Strong empirical results: the method not only outperforms other training-free methods by large margins but also matches or surpasses several training-based methods (e.g., outperforms VISA/VideoLISA on Ref-DAVIS and MeViS, and surpasses all training-based methods including an RL-trained Veason-R1 on ReasonVOS) despite requiring no training.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component (object-background contrasting, video-frame complementing, multi-scale fusion, rollout normalization, SAM prompting thresholds, attention consistency scoring), providing clear evidence for design choices.

Very extensive and honest appendix analysis, including failure case discussion, prompt robustness studies (showing the method is not overly sensitive to prompt phrasing), detailed reproduction analysis of baselines (Loc-Head, TAM) revealing their brittleness, part-level segmentation exploration, non-explicit/world-knowledge expression cases, and similar-multiple-object scenario comparisons with VRS-HQ.

The proposed attention-guided SAM2 prompting pipeline with tracklet scoring is a useful, generalizable contribution beyond the core fusion idea, effectively converting coarse attention into fine-grained masks without training a mask decoder.
Clear writing and figures that effectively illustrate the two fusion mechanisms and the overall pipeline.
weaknesses: The method involves multiple heuristic components (Gaussian smoothing, Otsu thresholding, several hand-tuned thresholds τpq, τtrk, NMS IoU threshold) whose interactions and sensitivity across arbitrary new datasets/models beyond those tested are not fully characterized, despite the threshold ablation provided.

Despite improvements, the approach still requires multiple additional MLLM forward passes per video (object-focused, background-focused, video-level, and per-frame prompts), and the paper does not report the computational/latency overhead compared to a single QA pass or to training-based baselines, which is relevant for a 'training-free' selling point that could still be inference-heavy.

On some referring-only benchmarks with less reasoning complexity (e.g., MeViS, Ref-YouTube-VOS), the method still noticeably trails state-of-the-art training-based methods (VRS-HQ, GLUS), somewhat tempering the 'comparable to training-based methods' claim to mainly the reasoning-heavy benchmarks.

The reliance on a single dominant object category extracted via prompting (object category choice prompt) may still struggle in genuinely ambiguous multi-object or multi-category referring scenarios, similar in spirit to the single-object limitation criticized in Loc-Head, though the paper provides some mitigating analysis.

Contour accuracy (F) of raw attention masks remains substantially lower than region similarity (J), indicating persistent boundary-precision limitations that are only partially resolved by the SAM2 stage.
